title: Lec 05 — Mitral Valve Disease
subtitle: Week 01 · Lec 05 · Mitral Valve Disease | 19 questions

questions.text: A 44-year-old woman who immigrated from a low-income country presents with three years of progressive exertional dyspnea. She recalls repeated episodes of sore throat during childhood that were never treated with antibiotics. Echocardiogram shows reduced mitral leaflet mobility, commissural fusion, and a valve area of 1.2 cm². Which of the following is the most likely cause of her mitral stenosis?
options: Rheumatic fever
Congenital bicuspid mitral valve
Carcinoid tumor
Eosinophilic endomyocardial fibroelastosis
questions.explanation:
Rheumatic fever is by far the most common cause of mitral stenosis. Untreated or inadequately treated group A streptococcal pharyngitis triggers an immune-mediated response that produces rheumatic fever; repeated episodes scar and fuse the mitral valve commissures over years, creating the characteristic narrowing. This patient's history of recurrent untreated pharyngitis in a resource-limited setting is the classic epidemiologic picture for rheumatic MS, which dominates the etiology list globally.
Option B is incorrect: congenital bicuspid mitral valve is a recognized but rare structural cause of MS that does not fit this epidemiologic context.
Option C is incorrect: carcinoid tumors can affect the mitral valve but are a rare non-rheumatic cause; carcinoid disease is listed among uncommon etiologies and is not suggested by this history.
Option D is incorrect: eosinophilic endomyocardial fibroelastosis is also listed as a rare non-rheumatic etiology; it is not the predominant cause and this history does not suggest it.
Slide 4 · Transcript 4:14

questions.text: Which of the following correctly describes the sequence of events that leads from an untreated respiratory infection to chronic rheumatic valve disease?
options: Viral pharyngitis → rheumatic fever → rheumatic heart disease
Streptococcal skin infection → rheumatic fever → mitral stenosis
Strep pharyngitis → rheumatic fever → rheumatic heart disease
Autoimmune arthritis → pericarditis → rheumatic valve disease
questions.explanation:
Group A streptococcal pharyngitis initiates the cascade: strep throat triggers rheumatic fever, which can progress to rheumatic heart disease. The immune response to the pharyngeal infection cross-reacts with cardiac tissue, causing the valve inflammation that underlies rheumatic heart disease. Streptococcal skin infections do not reliably trigger this cascade; only pharyngeal infection is established as the initiating event.
Option A is incorrect: viral pharyngitis does not cause rheumatic fever; the trigger is specifically group A streptococcal pharyngitis.
Option B is incorrect: streptococcal skin infections are not the recognized trigger for rheumatic fever; the site of infection matters.
Option D is incorrect: autoimmune arthritis progressing to pericarditis is not the mechanism of rheumatic heart disease taught in this lecture.
Slide 5 · Transcript 4:46

questions.text: Rheumatic heart disease is best classified as which of the following?
options: An isolated valvulitis affecting leaflet tissue only
A pancarditis involving the myocardium, valves, and pericardium
A myocarditis that spares the pericardium and valve leaflets
A fibrinous pericarditis occurring without valve involvement
questions.explanation:
Rheumatic heart disease is a pancarditis: it involves the myocardium, valves, and pericardium simultaneously. When rheumatic fever affects the heart, all three structural layers participate. The myocardium develops myocarditis, the valves develop valvulitis (the most clinically consequential component), and the pericardium can become inflamed as well. Recognizing it as a pancarditis explains why patients can present with multiple concurrent cardiac findings beyond just valve dysfunction.
Option A is incorrect: RHD is not confined to the valve leaflets; myocardial and pericardial involvement are integral parts of the disease.
Option C is incorrect: describing only myocarditis omits the pericardial and valvular components that define the pancarditis classification.
Option D is incorrect: fibrinous pericarditis alone without valve involvement is not an accurate characterization of RHD; the valve lesion is the hallmark.
Slide 11 · Transcript 10:58

questions.text: In rheumatic heart disease, which of the following best describes the typical temporal sequence of valvular lesions?
options: Aortic regurgitation develops first, followed later by tricuspid stenosis
Mitral stenosis appears first, followed subsequently by mitral regurgitation
Aortic insufficiency precedes both mitral valve lesions in the natural history
Mitral regurgitation develops first, with mitral stenosis appearing later
questions.explanation:
Mitral regurgitation is the earliest valvular lesion in rheumatic heart disease, with mitral stenosis developing later as scarring and fibrosis progress. Early rheumatic inflammation causes leaflet edema and dysfunction that produces regurgitation. Over subsequent years the leaflets thicken, calcify, and fuse at the commissures, converting the valve into a stenotic lesion. Aortic insufficiency develops eventually in roughly 20 to 40 percent of patients with rheumatic heart disease.
Option A is incorrect: aortic regurgitation is not the first lesion, and tricuspid stenosis in isolation is not the typical rheumatic sequence.
Option B is incorrect: the order is reversed here; MR precedes MS, not the other way around.
Option C is incorrect: aortic insufficiency is a later complication occurring in a subset of patients, not the initial valvular event.
Slide 11 · Transcript 11:36

questions.text:
A 51-year-old woman with mitral stenosis managed with diuretics for four years presents with sudden severe dyspnea and frothy sputum. Vital signs:
• Blood pressure: 94/62 mm Hg
• Pulse: 136/min, irregularly irregular
• Respiratory rate: 32/min
• O₂ saturation: 88% on room air
ECG shows atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. She was at her baseline yesterday. Which of the following mechanisms most directly accounts for her sudden deterioration?
options: Increased LV diastolic compliance reducing filling pressure and relieving congestion
Papillary muscle dysfunction from atrial stretch causing new mitral regurgitation
Loss of atrial kick and tachycardia-induced shortening of diastolic filling time
Acute right heart failure from pulmonary arterial vasoconstriction
questions.explanation:
Atrial fibrillation causes sudden decompensation in mitral stenosis through two simultaneous mechanisms: loss of atrial kick and tachycardia-induced shortening of diastolic filling time. The narrowed mitral valve already limits left ventricular filling to a slow, pressure-driven trickle during diastole. Atrial fibrillation eliminates the organized atrial contraction that provides the last increment of ventricular filling. Simultaneously, the rapid ventricular rate shortens the diastolic interval — the only period during which blood crosses the stenotic valve. Both effects sharply reduce LV preload and forward output while driving pressure back into the pulmonary veins.
Option A is incorrect: increased LV compliance would relieve congestion, not worsen it; in this scenario tachycardia narrows the diastolic window and worsens the gradient across the stenotic valve.
Option B is incorrect: papillary muscle dysfunction from atrial stretch is not the acute mechanism of AFib-triggered decompensation in MS as taught in this lecture.
Option D is incorrect: pulmonary arterial vasoconstriction is a chronic adaptive response that develops over time in MS; it is not the mechanism of acute AFib decompensation.
Slide 16 · Transcript 17:32

questions.text: Which of the following is a direct consequence of chronically elevated left atrial pressure in mitral stenosis?
options: Left ventricular concentric hypertrophy from elevated LV afterload
Aortic valve calcification from turbulent downstream flow
Right ventricular volume overload from increased pulmonary blood flow
Decreased pulmonary vascular resistance from hypoxia-induced vasodilation
Atrial fibrillation from left atrial dilation and wall stretch
questions.explanation:
Elevated left atrial pressure in MS causes left atrial dilation, and the resulting wall stretch drives the development of atrial fibrillation. As the stenotic mitral valve creates a sustained pressure load on the left atrium, the chamber enlarges progressively. Atrial stretch promotes electrical remodeling, ectopic pacemaker activity, and ultimately atrial fibrillation. The same elevated LA pressure also predisposes to blood stasis, thrombus formation, and systemic embolism — consequences that compound the risk once AFib develops.
Option A is incorrect: in MS the left ventricle is protected behind the stenotic valve; it receives less volume and does not experience elevated afterload leading to concentric hypertrophy.
Option B is incorrect: aortic valve calcification is an age-related degenerative process unrelated to elevated LA pressure in MS.
Option C is incorrect: MS restricts flow across the mitral valve and reduces, rather than increases, pulmonary blood volume. RV volume overload is not the expected consequence.
Option D is incorrect: pulmonary vascular resistance rises (not falls) as elevated venous pressure is transmitted to the pulmonary arterial bed; the end result is pulmonary arterial hypertension.
Slide 14 · Transcript 15:45

questions.text: In a patient with long-standing mitral stenosis and pulmonary arterial hypertension, what change to the right ventricle is expected?
options: Right ventricular atrophy from chronically reduced preload
Isolated right ventricular dilation without accompanying hypertrophy
Right ventricular fibrosis from ischemia as the dominant mechanism
RV hypertrophy and dilation from sustained pressure overload
questions.explanation:
Pulmonary arterial hypertension in MS imposes sustained pressure overload on the right ventricle, producing both hypertrophy and eventual dilation. The normal pulmonary arterial pressure is roughly 20 to 25 mmHg — far below systemic arterial pressure. As elevated left atrial pressure is transmitted backwards through the pulmonary veins into the pulmonary arterial system, the RV must pump against a progressively higher resistance. This pressure overload initially causes RV wall thickening (hypertrophy) and, as the ventricle begins to fail, chamber dilation follows.
Option A is incorrect: in MS-related PAH the RV faces elevated afterload, not reduced preload; atrophy is not the expected adaptive response.
Option B is incorrect: pressure overload produces hypertrophy in addition to eventual dilation; isolated dilation without hypertrophy is more typical of volume overload states.
Option C is incorrect: while ischemia can complicate RV failure at later stages, the primary mechanism taught here is pressure overload from PAH, not primary fibrotic ischemia.
Slide 14 · Transcript 16:12

questions.text:
A 42-year-old woman with a known mitral valve area of 1.1 cm² (normal ≥4.0 cm²) presents with hemoptysis — approximately three tablespoons of bright red blood. She has no fever and no productive cough. Vital signs:
• Temperature: 37.1°C
• WBC: 7,800/µL (normal 4,500–11,000/µL)
Chest X-ray shows left atrial enlargement but no focal infiltrate or consolidation. Which of the following best accounts for her hemoptysis?
options: Pulmonary abscess from aspiration pneumonia in an immunocompromised host
Elevated pulmonary venous pressure from the underlying mitral stenosis
Aortic dissection extending to the pulmonary artery
Pulmonary infarction from a thromboembolus
questions.explanation:
Hemoptysis is a recognized symptom of mitral stenosis, attributable to the chronically elevated pulmonary venous pressure caused by the obstructed mitral valve. The high-pressure pulmonary venous circulation engorges the bronchial vasculature; rupture of these congested vessels produces frank hemoptysis. The absence of fever, leukocytosis, and focal consolidation argues against an infectious or embolic cause.
Option A is incorrect: pulmonary abscess presents with fever, elevated white cell count, and a cavitating infiltrate — none of which are present here.
Option C is incorrect: aortic dissection extending to produce hemoptysis would present with acute-onset tearing pain and hemodynamic instability, not this stable, isolated bleeding picture.
Option D is incorrect: pulmonary embolism causing infarction typically produces pleuritic chest pain and a pleural-based opacity on imaging, which are absent in this case.
Slide 15 · Transcript 17:21

questions.text: A 56-year-old woman with a childhood history of rheumatic fever presents with two years of progressive dyspnea on exertion. She has no prior cardiac workup. On examination, she is placed in the left lateral decubitus position. Which set of auscultatory findings is most consistent with mitral stenosis?
options: Holosystolic murmur radiating to the axilla accompanied by a third heart sound (S3)
Systolic ejection murmur at the right second intercostal space radiating to the carotids
Low-pitched diastolic rumble at the cardiac apex preceded by an opening snap
High-pitched early diastolic decrescendo murmur along the left sternal border
questions.explanation:
Mitral stenosis produces a low-pitched diastolic rumble at the cardiac apex, characteristically preceded by an opening snap. The opening snap arises when the stiff, fused mitral leaflets abruptly halt at the limit of their tethered excursion as the valve opens in early diastole — a sudden stop in leaflet motion generates the snapping sound. The diastolic rumble that follows reflects turbulent flow crossing the narrowed orifice throughout diastole. Both sounds are best appreciated at the apex with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position.
Option A is incorrect: a holosystolic murmur radiating to the axilla with an S3 describes mitral regurgitation, not mitral stenosis.
Option B is incorrect: a systolic ejection murmur at the right second intercostal space radiating to the carotids is the hallmark of aortic stenosis.
Option D is incorrect: a high-pitched early diastolic decrescendo murmur along the left sternal border describes aortic regurgitation.
Slide 18 · Transcript 22:12

questions.text: Two patients each have mitral stenosis. Patient A has a mitral valve area of 1.8 cm²; Patient B has a mitral valve area of 0.9 cm². Compared to Patient A, which of the following auscultatory findings would be expected in Patient B?
options: A shorter interval between S2 and the opening snap
A longer interval between S2 and the opening snap
Absence of the opening snap due to leaflet calcification
An unchanged S2-OS interval with a louder diastolic rumble as the sole severity marker
questions.explanation:
More severe mitral stenosis produces a shorter S2-to-opening-snap (S2-OS) interval because higher left atrial pressure causes the mitral valve to snap open earlier in diastole. After aortic valve closure (S2), the mitral valve opens when left atrial pressure rises above the declining left ventricular diastolic pressure. With severe stenosis, LA pressure is substantially elevated and crosses the falling LV pressure sooner after S2, pulling the opening snap closer to the second heart sound. A shorter S2-OS interval therefore reflects higher LA pressure and more severe disease.
Option B is incorrect: a longer S2-OS interval would indicate lower LA pressure and milder disease — the opposite relationship.
Option C is incorrect: while heavy calcification can dampen or abolish the snap, absence of the opening snap is not the primary marker of severity taught in this lecture; the S2-OS interval is.
Option D is incorrect: the S2-OS interval changes with severity and is the key taught metric; murmur loudness alone is not the severity gauge here.
Slide 19 · Transcript 24:50

questions.text: A 63-year-old woman with long-standing mitral stenosis and known pulmonary hypertension presents for follow-up. Blood pressure is 126/76 mm Hg, pulse is 74/min and regular. Which of the following physical examination findings is most consistent with her pulmonary hypertension?
options: A laterally displaced apical impulse with an audible third heart sound (S3)
A right ventricular lift with a loud, accentuated pulmonic component of S2
A holosystolic murmur at the cardiac apex radiating toward the axilla
Muffled heart sounds with low voltage on the resting electrocardiogram
questions.explanation:
Pulmonary hypertension in MS produces an RV lift on palpation and a loud, accentuated P2 on auscultation. As pulmonary arterial pressure rises substantially, the hypertrophied right ventricle can be felt as a sternal or parasternal heave. The elevated pulmonary artery pressure causes the pulmonic valve to close with greater force, generating an accentuated P2. A loud P2 is therefore a clinical sign of pulmonary hypertension.
Option A is incorrect: a laterally displaced apical impulse with S3 reflects a dilated, volume-overloaded left ventricle — as in MR, not pure MS. A prominent LV impulse is actually inconsistent with isolated MS.
Option C is incorrect: a holosystolic murmur radiating to the axilla is the hallmark of mitral regurgitation, not a sign of pulmonary hypertension in MS.
Option D is incorrect: muffled heart sounds with low voltage suggest pericardial effusion, not pulmonary hypertension in the setting of MS.
Slide 18 · Transcript 19:55

questions.text: Compared to acute mitral regurgitation, which of the following best characterizes chronic mitral regurgitation?
options: High left atrial pressure with a small, non-compliant left atrium
Sudden dramatic onset with flash pulmonary edema and cardiogenic shock
Normal left atrial size with severe pulmonary venous congestion
A dilated, compliant left atrium with relatively less elevated pressure
questions.explanation:
Chronic MR is characterized by a dilated and relatively compliant left atrium that accommodates the regurgitant volume at a lower pressure than acute MR produces. In acute MR, the regurgitant volume suddenly floods a normal-sized, stiff left atrium; the sharp pressure rise causes flash pulmonary edema and shock. In chronic MR, the left atrium gradually enlarges and its wall becomes more distensible over time, accepting greater regurgitant volumes without proportional pressure elevation. As a result, patients with chronic MR can remain asymptomatic for years despite severe regurgitation.
Option A is incorrect: high LA pressure with a small, non-compliant LA describes acute MR, not chronic.
Option B is incorrect: sudden onset with flash pulmonary edema and shock is the presentation of acute, not chronic, MR.
Option C is incorrect: chronic MR is characterized by a dilated (not normal-sized) LA; the dramatic congestion of acute MR is absent in the adapted chronic state.
Slide 27 · Transcript 28:42

questions.text: A 67-year-old man develops flash pulmonary edema 48 hours after an inferior wall myocardial infarction. He is intubated and a pulmonary artery catheter is placed. Papillary muscle rupture is suspected as the cause. Which of the following catheter findings would be most expected?
options: Elevated right atrial pressure with a prominent X descent on the waveform
Low pulmonary capillary wedge pressure with a blunted V wave
Large V wave on the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure tracing
Step-up in oxygen saturation from the right atrium to the right ventricle
questions.explanation:
Acute MR from papillary muscle rupture produces a large V wave on the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) tracing. The PCWP reflects left atrial pressure. During each systole, the MR jet abruptly delivers the regurgitant volume into the non-compliant, undilated left atrium, generating a steep pressure spike — the V wave. This large V wave on the PCWP tracing is the hemodynamic hallmark of acute severe MR.
Option A is incorrect: a prominent X descent in the right atrial waveform points toward tricuspid regurgitation or right-sided pathology, not left-sided acute MR.
Option B is incorrect: the PCWP is elevated (not low) in acute MR because LA pressure rises sharply; the V wave contour is distinctly abnormal.
Option D is incorrect: an oxygen step-up from the right atrium to the right ventricle is the hemodynamic signature of a ventricular septal defect — a competing post-MI complication distinct from papillary muscle rupture.
Slide 28 · Slide 29 · Transcript 35:07

questions.text: In a patient with acute severe mitral regurgitation, the expected systolic murmur may be soft or even absent. Which of the following best explains this finding?
options: Destruction of the leaflets by endocarditis eliminates the orifice through which turbulence occurs
Rapid pressure equalization between the LV and the non-compliant LA eliminates the driving gradient
Systemic hypotension reduces aortic impedance sufficiently to prevent regurgitant flow
Tachycardia from sympathetic activation overlaps and obscures the systolic murmur
questions.explanation:
In acute MR, the non-compliant left atrium fills rapidly with regurgitant volume, driving LA pressure up toward LV systolic pressure; as the gradient narrows, the murmur shortens or disappears. A systolic murmur requires a sustained pressure difference across the mitral valve throughout systole. In acute MR the stiff, undilated LA cannot absorb the sudden volume without a sharp pressure rise. As LA pressure climbs toward LV systolic pressure, the gradient driving turbulent retrograde flow diminishes and may equalize before systole ends — shortening or obliterating the murmur.
Option A is incorrect: the presence or absence of leaflet tissue is not the primary determinant of murmur amplitude; the pressure gradient is. Significant murmurs can persist even through perforated leaflets as long as a gradient exists.
Option C is incorrect: systemic hypotension affects aortic impedance and changes LV work, but the murmur is determined by the LV-to-LA gradient, not by aortic pressures.
Option D is incorrect: tachycardia can shorten diastole and affect overall cardiac output, but it does not specifically eliminate the systolic murmur of MR.
Slide 28 · Transcript 33:44

questions.text: Which of the following best explains why the left ventricle in chronic mitral regurgitation is described as hyperdynamic?
options: Chronic adrenergic activation raises circulating catecholamines and increases myocardial inotropy
Increased preload from the regurgitant volume augments stroke volume via the Frank-Starling mechanism
Pulmonary hypertension reduces right ventricular output and unloads the left ventricle
Regurgitation into the low-pressure left atrium reduces LV afterload and allows hyperdynamic ejection
questions.explanation:
In chronic MR, the regurgitant pathway into the low-pressure left atrium acts as a pop-off valve that reduces the impedance against which the LV must eject, producing the hyperdynamic state. Because part of each stroke volume escapes through the mitral orifice into the low-resistance left atrium rather than exclusively through the high-resistance aorta, total LV wall stress during ejection falls. Lower afterload permits faster and more complete ejection, yielding a supranormal ejection fraction — a feature that paradoxically masks true LV dysfunction when EF appears “normal.”
Option A is incorrect: chronic sympathetic activation is not the primary mechanism taught for the hyperdynamic LV in chronic MR; the pop-off valve afterload reduction is.
Option B is incorrect: while preload does increase in chronic MR from the returning regurgitant volume, the hyperdynamic appearance is specifically explained by afterload reduction, not by Frank-Starling augmentation alone.
Option C is incorrect: pulmonary hypertension impairs RV function and can eventually reduce LV filling, but this is not the mechanism of hyperdynamic LV performance in early compensated chronic MR.
Slide 31 · Transcript 43:10

questions.text: A 61-year-old woman with severe chronic mitral regurgitation undergoes serial echocardiography. Her current left ventricular ejection fraction is 58% (reference range 55–70%). Which of the following best interprets this finding?
options: A normal EF signals impaired LV function; chronic MR should produce a supranormal EF
A normal EF confirms preserved LV contractile reserve because 58% falls within the reference range
Ejection fraction reliably identifies early LV dysfunction in MR because it corrects for altered loading
A mildly reduced EF would be expected at this stage; a preserved EF reflects early compensated disease
questions.explanation:
In severe chronic MR, a “normal” ejection fraction actually indicates impaired LV systolic function because the pop-off valve effect lowers afterload and the ventricle should be hyperdynamic with a supranormal EF. The reduced impedance of chronic MR means a healthy LV in this setting should eject with an EF well above the upper limit of the normal reference range. When the EF falls back into “normal” territory, it represents a substantial relative decline from the expected supranormal baseline — a sign that contractile reserve has been lost, not preserved.
Option B is incorrect: comparing this EF to a standard reference range is misleading in chronic MR; what looks normal is a warning sign in this context.
Option C is incorrect: ejection fraction does not reliably identify early LV dysfunction in MR precisely because it does not account for the altered loading conditions; the lecture explicitly states EF is not a good measure here.
Option D is incorrect: in early compensated chronic MR the EF should be supranormal, not mildly reduced; a mildly reduced EF would signify advanced, not early, dysfunction.
Slide 31 · Transcript 40:36

questions.text: Which of the following best describes the vicious cycle that perpetuates worsening mitral regurgitation in a patient with left ventricular dysfunction?
options: Pulmonary hypertension shifts the ventricular septum and impairs LV filling, reducing stroke volume
Elevated LA pressure triggers pulmonary vasoconstriction that reduces LV preload and accelerates failure
LV dilation worsens the regurgitant orifice, amplifying volume overload and driving further dilation
Atrial fibrillation reduces diastolic filling time, lowering LV output and promoting compensatory hypertrophy
questions.explanation:
The MR vicious cycle operates through a self-amplifying loop: LV dilation and dysfunction widen the mitral annulus and worsen the regurgitant orifice, which increases volume overload, which drives further dilation and dysfunction. As the left ventricle dilates from any cause — valve disease, ischemia, or cardiomyopathy — the mitral annulus widens and papillary muscles are displaced laterally, preventing complete leaflet coaptation. The resulting MR adds more regurgitant volume to each cycle, amplifying the volume overload and accelerating dilation. Each turn of the loop worsens the next.
Option A is incorrect: septal shift from pulmonary hypertension can impair LV filling (ventricular interdependence), but this is not the specific MR vicious cycle taught on this lecture’s slide.
Option B is incorrect: reflex pulmonary vasoconstriction reducing LV preload is not the mechanism of the MR feedback loop; LV volume overload from regurgitation is.
Option D is incorrect: atrial fibrillation and reduced filling time are relevant to MS decompensation but are not the LV dilation–MR feedback cycle depicted in this lecture.
Slide 34 · Transcript 46:47

questions.text: A 59-year-old man with chronic mitral regurgitation due to mitral valve prolapse reports mild fatigue but remains active. Blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg, pulse is 76/min. The point of maximal impulse (PMI) is displaced laterally and feels enlarged. Which additional auscultatory finding is most expected in this patient?
options: A mid-diastolic rumble with presystolic accentuation at the cardiac apex
A holosystolic murmur at the cardiac apex with radiation toward the axilla
A crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border with a delayed carotid upstroke
A high-pitched decrescendo murmur along the left sternal border beginning immediately after S2
questions.explanation:
Chronic MR produces a holosystolic murmur at the cardiac apex, and the laterally displaced enlarged PMI reflects LV dilation from the chronic volume load. The LV-to-LA pressure gradient persists throughout systole, generating continuous turbulent flow through the incompetent mitral orifice — hence a holosystolic (pansystolic) murmur. Importantly, murmur intensity does not correlate with the severity of the regurgitant flow; a soft murmur does not indicate mild disease.
Option A is incorrect: a mid-diastolic rumble with presystolic accentuation is the murmur of mitral stenosis, not mitral regurgitation.
Option C is incorrect: a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border with a delayed carotid upstroke is the hallmark of aortic stenosis.
Option D is incorrect: a high-pitched decrescendo murmur along the left sternal border beginning at S2 describes aortic regurgitation.
Slide 32 · Transcript 38:43

questions.text: A 45-year-old man with a history of bacterial endocarditis (treated two years ago and fully resolved) is scheduled for two upcoming procedures: a tooth extraction next week and a colonoscopy the week after. According to this lecture's teaching on endocarditis prophylaxis, which of the following correctly describes the prophylaxis requirements?
options: Both procedures require prophylaxis because prior endocarditis is a high-risk cardiac condition
Neither procedure requires prophylaxis because the endocarditis resolved more than 6 months ago
Prophylaxis is needed only for the colonoscopy; GI procedures carry the highest bacteremia risk
Only the dental extraction requires prophylaxis; the indication applies to oral procedures only
questions.explanation:
Prior endocarditis is a high-risk cardiac condition that warrants endocarditis prophylaxis — but the critical restriction is that prophylaxis is indicated only for oral (dental) procedures, not gastrointestinal or genitourinary procedures. The tooth extraction falls within the oral procedure indication, so prophylaxis is appropriate. The colonoscopy is a GI procedure; regardless of the patient’s cardiac risk, prophylaxis is not indicated before GI procedures as taught in this lecture.
Option A is incorrect: although prior endocarditis does qualify as a high-risk condition, prophylaxis for the colonoscopy is not indicated because it is a GI, not an oral, procedure.
Option B is incorrect: prior endocarditis is a permanent indication for prophylaxis before dental procedures; resolution of the infection does not remove this designation.
Option C is incorrect: the prophylaxis indication covers oral procedures, not GI procedures — so if anything, the dental procedure requires prophylaxis, not the colonoscopy.
Slide 40 · Transcript 51:30
